items.title: Syntha now runs deals across multiple legal entities
items.summary: Syntha now runs deals across multiple legal entities. In fashion wholesale, a brand, a distributor and a production partner almost never operate through one legal entity, especially when foreign counterparties are in the chain.
items.content_text:
Syntha now runs deals across multiple legal entities. In fashion wholesale, a brand, a distributor and a production partner almost never operate through one legal entity, especially when foreign counterparties are in the chain.

Syntha has a legal-entity registry. You can set up Russian and foreign details and run a deal under the right entity, instead of one shared company profile.

• A brand with several legal entities runs deals under each of them. · A partner in another jurisdiction works in the same system as everyone else. · Details of Russian and foreign legal entities are kept in one registry.

items.title: In Renova, an enquiry becomes a project in a single step
items.summary: In Renova, an enquiry becomes a project in a single step. Until now a renovation lead and a working project were only loosely connected: turning an enquiry into a project with a contractor, a client and a schedule meant checking by hand who was who.
items.content_text:
In Renova, an enquiry becomes a project in a single step. Until now a renovation lead and a working project were only loosely connected: turning an enquiry into a project with a contractor, a client and a schedule meant checking by hand who was who.

Managing project participants and converting a lead into active work now happen as a single operation. It has been tested under simultaneous use: two sessions at once do not drift apart in the data. The core mechanism is built and tested; completing the independent-contractor flow is in progress.

• An enquiry becomes a project without manual checking. · Records of who runs a site no longer get lost at the seam between lead and project. · Two people can work on one project at once without conflicts.

items.title: ChatX now has a company wiki
items.summary: ChatX now has a company wiki. Knowledge is usually kept everywhere except the messenger: pinned messages, files on a drive, in the heads of the longest-serving staff.
items.content_text:
ChatX now has a company wiki. Knowledge is usually kept everywhere except the messenger: pinned messages, files on a drive, in the heads of the longest-serving staff.

A shared wiki – pages the whole team can edit, with full edit history. You can see who changed what and roll back to an earlier version.

• A decision or process discussed in a channel is kept alongside it, not in a separate service. · Knowledge is not tied to one person. · Any edit can be rolled back.

items.title: Material purchasing now runs inside Syntha
items.summary: Material purchasing now runs inside Syntha. Previously, the supplier request, quote, approval and order were handled manually, outside the system that already holds the specification and the collection volume.
items.content_text:
Material purchasing now runs inside Syntha. Previously, the supplier request, quote, approval and order were handled manually, outside the system that already holds the specification and the collection volume.

The price request, supplier quote, award and material purchase order run as one chain inside Syntha, on the same data as the spec. The chain is available in the Syntha interface and through the API.

• The supplier is chosen on numbers already in the system, not a separate spreadsheet. · Material cost comes from the purchasing process itself, not from a reconciliation afterwards. · Fabric and trims are no longer handled outside the system.

items.title: ChatX now suggests what to reply
items.summary: ChatX now suggests what to reply. Coming back to a chat after a meeting and working out what happened over two hours takes real effort, and writing a substantive reply rather than “ok, will check” is harder still.
items.content_text:
ChatX now suggests what to reply. Coming back to a chat after a meeting and working out what happened over two hours takes real effort, and writing a substantive reply rather than “ok, will check” is harder still.

An AI assistant is built into the conversation. It summarises the thread and suggests replies based on context. Nothing is sent without a person’s confirmation.

• A summary instead of reading two hours of messages. · A substantive reply ready in seconds. · The decision stays with the person writing.

items.title: Renova stops losing actions when the connection drops
items.summary: Renova no longer loses actions when the connection drops. On a site or on the road, connectivity fails regularly. If the app was sending an action at that moment – sign off a stage, confirm a payment – it must neither be lost nor run twice.
items.content_text:
Renova no longer loses actions when the connection drops. On a site or on the road, connectivity fails regularly. If the app was sending an action at that moment – sign off a stage, confirm a payment – it must neither be lost nor run twice.

Queued actions are protected against repeats and against drift between sessions. Resending after a dropped connection does not duplicate the result.

• A signed-off stage or a confirmed payment survives a dropped connection. · Resending does not create a duplicate. · Sessions on different devices do not overwrite each other’s state.

items.title: Stores count in days, brands in seasons
items.summary: The data behind collection decisions arrives later than the decisions are due. A season runs three to six months, and the summary of it is put together at the end.
items.content_text:
The data behind collection decisions arrives later than the decisions are due. A season runs three to six months, and the summary of it is put together at the end.

Retail sees every sale on the till and can reprice tomorrow. A brand counts in seasons: product in one system, sales in partners’ reports, stock in a spreadsheet. It can be reconciled by hand, but by the time the picture is ready the season is closed. The price of the gap is concrete. A markdown called a week late gives away margin on every unit. A reorder placed after the factory’s window has closed means lost sales on a bestseller. Stock spotted only at period close is cash that could have worked in the next buy.

Syntha puts collection plan, assortment, order, confirmation and shipment into one loop. A pricing, reorder or exit decision is available while it can still change the outcome of the season. · Markdowns and reorders rest on current data, not the quarter’s report. · No new team is needed: data that already exists meets on time. · Stock is visible before period close, so capital returns to buying sooner.

items.title: Inditex: revenue up 8.4%, ahead of forecasts, but profit misses
items.summary: At Inditex (Zara), sales growth and profit growth have parted ways: costs are outrunning revenue. For a brand owner, it is a prompt to check exactly what you are paying for when sales rise.
items.content_text:
At Inditex (Zara), sales growth and profit growth have parted ways: costs are outrunning revenue. For a brand owner, it is a prompt to check exactly what you are paying for when sales rise.

Bloomberg reports that Inditex revenue grew 8.4% at constant currency, to €9.8bn. Analysts had expected 7–8%. Operating profit fell short of expectations: costs grew faster than revenue. Over two years the company invested €1.8bn in logistics and added a further €200m of capital spending to modernise its head office.

Strong revenue with a weak margin looks like an investment phase, not a demand problem. The money goes into capacity that serves delivery speed and supply-chain flexibility. The payoff from spending like this shows up later, not in the same quarter. One quarter cannot tell you whether the bet will pay back, so the margin trend in coming reports is what matters.

The calm reading, “it’s investment”, should not be mistaken for a guarantee. Revenue already beats forecasts, so profit now decides how the company is judged. If the next quarters show no return to margin, the cost growth will be read as lost control rather than strategy. Treating Inditex as a model for a small brand is risky: its scale of spending is out of reach, but the logic of the test still applies.

• Break down your cost increase over the latest period: how much is investment, how much is lost efficiency. · For each large capital item, name a payback metric and the quarter in which you expect margin to recover. · Watch Inditex’s margin in coming reports: it will show whether the logistics bet has paid off.

items.title: Italian fashion exports: −2.3% on average, but from +6.8% in Hong Kong to −9.6% in Japan
items.summary: Italian fashion revenue in 2026 is expected at €91.4bn. That is 1.6% below last year but well ahead of the first forecast. The story is not the total but the spread between countries.
items.content_text:
Italian fashion revenue in 2026 is expected at €91.4bn. That is 1.6% below last year but well ahead of the first forecast. The story is not the total but the spread between countries.

The forecast had been an 8.5% fall; now the expected drop is 1.6%. Exports of core categories fell 2.3% from January to May. France (+3.7%), Spain (+4.5%) and Hong Kong (+6.8%) are growing. The US (−2.8%), Germany (−4.2%), the UK (−8.8%) and Japan (−9.6%) are falling. Textile and clothing production dropped 7.1% year-on-year in June.

The average is built from opposite movements, and the gap between the extreme markets is about 16 percentage points. Two brands with identical product can post results of opposite sign if one sells to Japan and the other to Hong Kong. So the industry trend says nothing about any single company. The June output fall of 7.1% is a separate signal: it is steeper than the export decline and may mean factories are cutting output before sales fall.

The reader’s main mistake is to take “−2.3%” as a mild, even dip that everyone can plan around. The piece does not explain why the markets diverge, and these numbers do not support any guess at the cause. For decisions, though, the cause is not needed: it is enough to know your own markets may sit at opposite ends of this range. A caveat: the data covers five months, and the picture may change by year-end.

• Break your exports down by country and compare them with these figures: are you in the growing group or the falling one? · For Japan and the UK, find the cause of any decline in your own sales before cutting back presence. · For Hong Kong, Spain and France, estimate how much extra volume you could ship without losing margin. · Build the risk of slowing factories into your buying calendar: June’s 7.1% production fall points to it.

items.title: A Vietnamese seamstress costs three times her Bangladeshi peer – and factories are answering with robots
items.summary: Vietnam pays a seamstress about $300 a month and is not trying to cut that pay: it is raising output instead. For a buyer, the question shifts from “where is it cheapest?” to “where is it faster and steadier?”
items.content_text:
Vietnam pays a seamstress about $300 a month and is not trying to cut that pay: it is raising output instead. For a buyer, the question shifts from “where is it cheapest?” to “where is it faster and steadier?”

Ascentium examines an industry that ranks third in the world for clothing exports, after China and Bangladesh. A seamstress earns about $300 a month in Vietnam, $95 in Bangladesh and $145 in India. Factories are adopting AI, robotics and modern sewing systems, and one worker with new equipment produces 4–5 times more. The industry aims to cut labour cost per unit by 30–40%. Exports rose from $35bn in 2020 to $46bn in 2025, with a 2026 target of $47–48bn.

This is automation for survival in a price race, not for cutting headcount. Vietnam cannot match Bangladesh on wages, so it squeezes labour cost out of each unit. There is a ceiling, though: the country imports 95–100% of its cotton and synthetics. Robots lower the cost of sewing, not the cost of fabric, which stays with foreign suppliers. The gain shows up in the price of the work, not in the price of the finished garment.

Most readers will see “Vietnam is catching up on price”. I read it differently: it is choosing another niche, one that pays for speed and consistent quality rather than the lowest price. Export growth alongside rising wages suggests the bet is working so far. The risk is that the 30–40% cut is still the industry’s stated target, not a proven result.

• Recalculate the unit cost of an order across all three countries using the expected fall in Vietnamese labour cost, not today’s rate. · Split the collection: keep price-driven basics in Bangladesh or India, and assess in Vietnam the styles where lead time and repeatable quality matter. · Add the Vietnamese factories’ reliance on imported fabric to your risk register and check where your own material comes from.

items.title: £3.9bn a year: what UK retail loses on goods never meant for sale
items.summary: Drapers has estimated a hidden cost line in British fashion retail. If it is not a separate line in your P&L, you probably do not know your own figure.
items.content_text:
Drapers has estimated a hidden cost line in British fashion retail. If it is not a separate line in your P&L, you probably do not know your own figure.

Goods never intended for sale – damaged in transit, written off, irreparable defects – cost British fashion retail around £3.9bn a year, by the publication’s estimate. Meanwhile, 84% of retailers name staffing costs as their biggest concern going into 2026, and the sector’s growth forecast for the year is 2.3%.

Such losses dissolve into cost of goods and logistics, so they never show in a standard P&L. They do show in working capital: cash is tied up in stock that will never become revenue. With the market growing at 2.3%, recovering even part of the sum may do more than a new marketing campaign.

The figure matters because it is not a forecast or a risk estimate – it is money already spent. It is easy to read as a British problem, but the mechanism is universal: what is not counted separately is not managed. A caveat: the Drapers figure is an industry-wide estimate, and an individual brand’s share of losses may differ widely.

• Set up a separate accounting line for goods not meant for sale: transit damage, write-offs, irreparable defects. · Calculate that line as a percentage of last year’s purchases. · Find the three biggest causes and fix the costliest one with your carrier or supplier. · Review this line before cutting headcount in response to rising staffing costs.

items.title: Japan’s online fashion market to grow from $32.4bn to $86.2bn by 2033
items.summary: Nearly every adult in Japan already has internet and a smartphone, yet the market is still growing 15.2% a year. For a brand eyeing Japan, the question is not whether shoppers can reach your site but how you plug into local channels.
items.content_text:
Nearly every adult in Japan already has internet and a smartphone, yet the market is still growing 15.2% a year. For a brand eyeing Japan, the question is not whether shoppers can reach your site but how you plug into local channels.

Coherent Market Insights values the market at $32.4bn in 2026 and $86.2bn by 2033, a 15.2% compound annual growth rate. Internet penetration is 93% among adults, smartphone penetration 85%. The drivers it names: global brands moving into Japanese online retail, fast-growing social commerce, omnichannel (click-and-collect, moving between online and offline) and AR/VR try-on.

Double-digit growth usually appears where infrastructure is still catching up with demand. Here it is already in place, and the market still grows. So the fuel is not access to the network but how people buy: through social platforms, in-store collection, a blend of online and shop. Translating the storefront removes only the first barrier. The rest are operational: platforms, logistics, pick-up points.

Most readers will take this as “huge market, let’s go”. I read it differently: the market is growing alongside global brands, and share goes to whoever assembles a local operating chain first. That is my reading; the report does not state it outright. If it turns out the growth is mostly driven by a few big platforms, a smaller brand may need just one partner.

• Cost a Japan launch as an operations project – social platforms, logistics, returns – not as a website translation. · Check which social-commerce and click-and-collect channels your closest rivals in Japan use. · Pilot AR/VR try-on in one category before budgeting it across the range. · Plan over several years: the forecast covers the whole category, not your share of it.

items.title: From 19 July 2026, the EU bans destroying unsold clothing
items.summary: An ESPR requirement stops being a plan and becomes law, with an exact date. For a brand selling into the EU, it changes how leftover stock is handled right now.
items.content_text:
An ESPR requirement stops being a plan and becomes law, with an exact date. For a brand selling into the EU, it changes how leftover stock is handled right now.

From 19 July 2026, large companies in the EU may not destroy unsold clothing, footwear and accessories. Detailed requirements for the textile Digital Product Passport are expected by the end of 2027. It becomes mandatory roughly 18 months after they are adopted, around 2028–2029. From 19 July 2030, the destruction ban extends to medium-sized companies (50–249 employees).

The two rules run on different clocks. The destruction ban applies in 2026 and hits leftover stock: what used to be written off must now be sold, donated or recycled. The product passport needs data on composition and supply chain. If a brand has never collected it, it will have to be gathered from suppliers, and that takes time. So 18 months after the requirements appear will be short for anyone starting from zero.

It is a mistake to read 2027–2028 as “too early”. The passport deadline is not a starting point; it is the date to count backwards from. The source gives no timeline for gathering supplier data; that estimate is mine, resting on the fact that data a brand has never collected cannot be obtained quickly.

• Size the stock you used to write off and line up channels for it: outlet, donation, recycling. · List the composition and supplier data you need for each category and mark what is missing. · Ask key suppliers which data they can already provide. · If you employ 50–249 people, put 19 July 2030 in the plan as your own deadline.

items.title: 46% of fashion executives expect 2026 to worsen, up from 39% a year ago
items.summary: McKinsey and BoF report that pessimism is rising for a third year running. For a brand owner, that means planning without waiting for things to “clear up”.
items.content_text:
McKinsey and BoF report that pessimism is rising for a third year running. For a brand owner, that means planning without waiting for things to “clear up”.

46% of executives expect conditions to worsen in 2026, against 39% a year ago. Tariffs and trade barriers are the top risk for 76%. AI has overtaken sustainability as the leading growth priority for the first time. Resale is growing two to three times faster than the primary market through 2027, jewellery almost four times faster than clothing, and the mid-price segment is outpacing luxury as a source of growth.

It is not only anxiety that is rising but the reallocation of money. Growth is moving out of luxury and new collections into the mid-market, jewellery and resale. These are different business models, with different margins and stock turn. So waiting it out is not an option: while a brand waits for clarity, capital and customers have already moved.

A report like this gets read selectively: people pick out the AI figure or the tariff figure and overlook the rest. What matters most to me is the change of regime. Three years of rising pessimism is not a cycle but a new normal, and budgets should be built on scenarios. A caveat: the survey captures sentiment, not results, and an individual brand can still beat the market.

• Split the 2026 buying budget into base, downside and upside scenarios. · Calculate the tariff impact on the cost of each category and line up backup suppliers. · Test resale or a mid-price line with a single capsule, without waiting for the numbers to confirm it. · Set a buying-review date every quarter instead of waiting for “clarity”.

items.title: 400–500 clothing stores closed in a year as the empty-shelves boost fades
items.summary: In 2025, 400–500 clothing stores closed in Russia. For a brand, that marks the end of easy mall space and the start of real bargaining with landlords.
items.content_text:
In 2025, 400–500 clothing stores closed in Russia. For a brand, that marks the end of easy mall space and the start of real bargaining with landlords.

Around 25 brands also left. Mall vacancy could rise from 7.7% to 9.7%, according to CORE.XP. Just 12 new international brands entered in 2025, against more than 20 a year before; Turkey’s AC& and Mudo have already gone, citing weak demand and competition. Eterna’s chief executive, Dmitry Tomilin, calls 2026 “a year of survival”. The causes: demand is shifting to essentials, costs are climbing, retailers have run out of reserves and landlords are under pressure to cut rents.

In 2022–2023, dozens of new brands moved into the space left by Zara, Mango and H&M. Empty shelves in the malls handed them footfall for little effort, and many budgeted for the usual two-to-three-year retail payback. Now they have to earn that traffic, and weak economics show at once. The closures are a shakeout of projects launched on a window of opportunity, not a verdict on the whole industry.

Many will read the numbers as a signal to retreat. I read them the other way: landlords facing rising vacancy are willing to negotiate for the first time in years. Brands with proven unit economics stand to gain. The risk lies elsewhere: consumer demand is softening, and cheaper rent will not save a store that does not sell.

• Recalculate each store’s payback without assuming free mall footfall. · Ask landlords for lower rents and shorter leases – with vacancy rising, you have leverage. · Rebuild the 2026 range with more core basics, as demand shifts towards essentials. · Before taking over space left by AC& and Mudo, find out why their model failed.

items.title: 92% of fashion companies are raising AI budgets, and only 1% call their projects mature
items.summary: Almost the whole industry is putting money into AI, yet hardly anyone has a mature project. For a brand owner, that means the gap to competitors is smaller than their press releases suggest.
items.content_text:
Almost the whole industry is putting money into AI, yet hardly anyone has a mature project. For a brand owner, that means the gap to competitors is smaller than their press releases suggest.

In the McKinsey and Business of Fashion “State of Fashion 2026” report, 35% of fashion executives say they already use generative AI: for customer service, images, copy and product search. 92% of organisations plan to increase investment. Only 1% call their AI rollout projects “mature”. Market Research Future estimates the AI-in-fashion market will grow from $5.9bn in 2025 to nearly $30bn by 2034.

The 92% and the 1% describe one picture: money is flowing to where results are not yet proven. So a loud announcement of AI adoption says little about outcomes; for most companies these are still pilots. The winner is not whoever announced first but whoever takes one pilot to a measurable result and carries it across other processes.

The real risk is not falling behind, as many headlines suggest, but wasting budget on a broad “AI programme” with no metric. When almost nobody has a mature example, there is nothing to copy, and every brand has to be judged on its own numbers. The 1% may also understate reality: companies may simply be grading themselves harshly.

• Pick one task where AI is already in use: customer service, product search, copy or images. · Set its metric before launch: response time, search conversion, cost per product description. · Check competitors’ AI claims against actual results, not announcements. · Build in a stop point: if a quarter passes with no effect in the numbers, rethink the project.

items.title: China’s luxury market in 2026: six shifts, and none is about “young and digital”
items.summary: Jing Daily names six consumer shifts in Chinese luxury for 2026. Together they break the familiar buyer profile: young, digital, fond of “quiet luxury”.
items.content_text:
Jing Daily names six consumer shifts in Chinese luxury for 2026. Together they break the familiar buyer profile: young, digital, fond of “quiet luxury”.

Fitness and wellness open a route into luxury through sports brands. Short dramas on Douyin replace classic influencers as an ad format. Maximalism returns after “quiet luxury”. Women over 40 become a visible buying force. Gold jewellery made with traditional techniques grows as its own category. Buyers expect instant delivery even for luxury goods.

These six shifts do not add up to one portrait. Each has its own audience and channel: the sportswoman, the Douyin drama viewer, the mature woman, the craft connoisseur. The market is splitting into segments, and a brand that speaks to everyone in one voice reaches none of them. Hence the odd pairing: maximalism is back just as Western houses finished tailoring collections to “quiet luxury”.

The riskiest mistake is to read this as a list of trends to bolt onto a lookbook. It signals that the average Chinese buyer has stopped existing. Winners will sort their customers into segments before competitors do; losers will chase maximalism with last year’s creative. One caveat: this is a press review, not sales data, and it does not measure the size of each segment.

• Check which of the six groups your China campaigns actually target, and work out the budget share for each. · Test Douyin short dramas on a single capsule before moving influencer budget there. · Build a separate maximalist line for China without touching the global collection. · Find out from your customer base how many buyers are over 40 and what they buy.

items.title: What Grazia asked about the future of fashion
items.summary: Grazia asked fashion experts what the industry will look like in five years, following the BRICS+ Fashion Summit. I was quoted first among those invited. My answer: the brands that win will be the ones that combine creative instinct with precise calculation.
items.content_text:
Grazia asked fashion experts what the industry will look like in five years, following the BRICS+ Fashion Summit. I was quoted first among those invited. My answer: the brands that win will be the ones that combine creative instinct with precise calculation.

The magazine asked several experts where fashion is heading over a five-year horizon – from materials and production to how business decisions get made.

My answer was about data: “The fashion industry still runs on intuition and visual instinct, but the future belongs to data. The brands that win will be the ones that combine creative instinct with precise calculation.” Calculation does not cancel the idea; it tests it before a batch is bought.

• Mark which collection decisions you make on instinct and which on numbers. · For recurring decisions – buying, pricing, reordering – set the measure you check them against. · Test the collection idea against the numbers before buying, not after the season.
